content: Young children experiencing acute diarrhoea, often caused by infectious gastroenteritis, may temporarily lose the ability to produce lactase, the enzyme responsible for digesting lactose. This can lead to an inability to properly digest lactose, the primary sugar found in milk, which may exacerbate or prolong the diarrhoeal illness. There is ongoing uncertainty about whether avoiding lactose-containing milk or milk products can help these children recover more quickly. The objective of this study was to determine whether avoiding or reducing the intake of lactose-containing milk or milk products could shorten the duration and severity of acute diarrhoea in young children. Additionally, the study aimed to evaluate other indicators of morbidity and overall mortality. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to May 14, 2013. References from relevant trials, key conference proceedings, and communications with experts in the field were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed the effects of avoiding or reducing lactose exposure in children under five years of age with acute diarrhoea. Data were extracted using standardized methods, and trial quality was independently assessed by two reviewers. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MD), while dichotomous outcomes were evaluated using risk ratios (RR). All results were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The analysis included 33 trials involving 2973 children with acute diarrhoea. Most of these trials (29) were conducted in inpatient settings within highor middle-income countries. Fifteen trials included children under 12 months of age, while 22 trials excluded breast-fed children. The findings suggest that lactose-free products may reduce the duration of diarrhoea by an average of approximately 18 hours compared to lactose-containing milk, milk products, or foodstuffs (MD -17.77 hours, 95% CI -25.32 to -10.21, based on 16 trials with 1467 participants; low-quality evidence). Additionally, lactose-free products likely reduce the risk of treatment failure, defined variably as persistent or worsening diarrhoea or vomiting, the need for additional rehydration therapy, or continued weight loss, by about 50% (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.68, based on 18 trials with 1470 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Diluted lactose-containing milk, when compared to undiluted milk or milk products, did not demonstrate a reduction in the duration of diarrhoea (based on five trials with 417 participants; low-quality evidence). However, it may reduce the risk of treatment failure (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.94, based on nine trials with 687 participants; low-quality evidence). In conclusion, for young children with acute diarrhoea who are not predominantly breast-fed, switching to a lactose-free diet may lead to faster resolution of diarrhoea and a lower risk of treatment failure. Diluting lactose-containing formulas may also offer some benefits, but further research is needed to confirm these findings. Importantly, no trials were conducted in low-income countries, where diarrhoea-related mortality and malnutrition are more prevalent.
